title: 🩸 Red dye might not be enough
body_text: Being in the hospital is stressful enough, whether you’re a patient, loved one of a patient, or a staff member. And there’s one thing that sets everyone in a hospital even more on edge: the relentless, never-ending, cacophony of beeps. Most of the beeping beeps and ringing alarms don’t actually mean anyone needs to do anything – cue Homer Simpson’s sonically abusive invention, the deafening " Everything is OK alarm ” – which means doctors and nurses tend to tune them out. In most cases, that’s not a problem, but when it is a problem, it’s a problem . So, The Wall Street Journal reports , a Stanford University hospital sorted through the whole gamut of audible alerts in the monitoring equipment it uses and worked to cut out those that were unactionable or likely to quickly and harmless self-correct. The result? As much as a whooping 82% reduction in beeps. Even better, nurses said that they were better at actually responding to patient needs. Stocks dropped on Monday as Treasury yields rose. If you’ve driven a Ford – or any other type of internal combustion vehicle – lately , you’ve probably noticed that gas is expensive. Really expensive. Prices at the pump are up almost $1.50 per gallon since the US attacked Iran in late February. Things look even worse if you drive a truck, tractor or anything that runs on diesel, with the national average price per gallon sitting at $6.45, per AAA . Before the war, a gallon of diesel was just $3.75 . Diesel’s surge is pushing transportation and farming costs higher, contributing to the persistently high inflation that is the bane of politicians, consumers, and central bankers alike. To bring diesel prices down, the White House tried seeking voluntary diesel export limits from refiners last week, Reuters reported . Beyond asking nicely, a full export ban has also been mulled, not least by President Donald Trump, who took his own administration somewhat by surprise by publicly saying he supported the idea . Also gaining traction in the White House: slashing taxes on so-called red dyed diesel. Federal taxes for regular, un-dyed diesel sit at just under a quarter a gallon. Red-dyed diesel, which is distinguished by the addition of – you guessed it – red dye, can only be used in off-road activities like farming and power generation, is subject to a mere penny a gallon federal tax. The idea under consideration is to allow red dyed diesel to be used for on-road vehicles. A full-scale ban on diesel exports would likely lead rather quickly to domestic oversupply, which would cause refiners to cut production, leading rather quickly to scarcity domestically while drastically reducing supplies in Europe, industry officials have argued. Allowing wider use of red-dyed diesel might not have much of an effect on prices. "I can't ⁠think that this would have any impact at all," Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, told Reuters . "It's simply diesel with red dye added that's not taxed. title: 🌟 Zuck Finds His Muse
body_text: When companies wanted to get their trashcans and bear bags approved as “bear-resistant,” they had to go through “Kobuk the Destroyer,” a captive grizzly bear employed by the testing industry to see how good the bear-safe tech actually was. Kobuk is one bright bear, capable of solving clever bearproofing not merely by brute force but also by intelligently manipulating the device with his shockingly nimble claws. Don’t get it twisted, though: “The Destroyer” was so named not because of any ursine brutality but rather because he destroyed the hopes and dreams of many inventors of sub-par anti-bear tech. Stocks closed up on Friday, capping off a solid week for equity markets. Meta ’s stock finished last week up 13% on the heels of the release of Muse, which is the company’s big play to try to get consumers using AI in their day-to-day lives. Lots of the earliest applications of AI were in coding; LLMs trained on every StackOverflow and GitHub page turned out to be rather canny programmers, which is one reason that some of the earliest adopters and advocates were in tech, amazed that the madlibs machine was pretty good at writing code. The emergence of ChatGPT was a milestone because it demonstrated that the LLMs had applications replacing certain features of search engines, which lots of consumers use day-to-day, and which launched the tech into the mainstream. Still, lots of the actual applications of this stuff — the things that moved markets — were people at companies using AI tools to write code faster, more effectively, and to scale up projects that would have required engineering resources more quickly. This is one reason we saw so much disruption in the SaaS space, as those companies began to worry that their clients could make Claude write the program that they were on retainer to produce Other uses remained firmly in the industrial or scientific space; image models are good at spotting anomalies, at processing large amounts of data, and so on, and so we began to see promising developments in things like archaeology, astronomy, and other fields where there were enormous piles of data and not enough time or money to sift through it. That’s all well and good, but you don’t get to be a trillion dollar industry by selling software to archaeologists. The grail is and was: how do we get consumers relying on this thing multiple times per day? And one solution was not just new and better models, but an effective harness that consumers would actually use. Those early adopters in the tech scene — the ones who saw the appeal of AI tools in their coding jobs — became enamored with a tool called OpenClaw, which allowed these nerds to build self-hosted systems on Apple Mac Minis that were connected by Telegram and have it actually do stuff like make dinner reservations and write emails. With a harness like that, you can make AI models do things that they otherwise aren’t able to do, making them more powerful in the specific applications you might want them to do by offering a set of rules and tools that they can reliably use rather than hallucinating reactions on the fly. They’re rather neat, and can be a missing link between a chatbot and a piece of software that can get you new car insurance. Most normies do not have a spare Mac Mini, they are insufficiently Russian to have Telegram on their phone, and they don’t have time to deal with this. There is a reason that nobody asked you to fix their OpenClaw setup or reset their Hermes password last year at Thanksgiving. Meta in particular saw this opportunity. They realized that perhaps no company in the tech space has as much insight into the, shall we say, unique technological disposition of the median internet user . Salt-of-the-earth types. You catch my meaning. They set out to make a harness for the masses, an “OpenClaw” that — with an appropriate amount of handholding, the kind of built-in security measures that you design when you believe core customer struggles to open Tylenol bottles, and a mascot that looks like a Republican Labubu — you could be the one to bring AI to the masses even if your AI models were middle-of-the-pack. This worked pretty well for them, as Muse is a big ol’ hit. But the launch revealed one key thing. The success or failure of a given AI product these days isn’t actually all that related to the power of the model underneath it. Muse is a harness for that model, and appears to have impressed enough consumers out of the gate to propel its app to the top of the charts. But the launch revealed another thing that will decide whether your AI product will actually catch on: a surprisingly large part of this is going to come down to the simple question of how much the companies you interact with want to deal with Meta. Take, for instance, a key use of Muse, which is that it should be able to buy stuff for you. One can imagine a very convenient scenario where you tell Muse that you want to buy more laundry detergent and it goes ahead and orders it for you after shopping around for the best price. But, you and Muse a ren’t the only one involved in that transaction ; it’s contingent on Amazon or Walmart, both of which have their own shopping AI, being willing to play ball. The week it launched, Muse got a bit of air taken out of it when Amazon announced that it’s blocking the thing from its website. Amazon does not want Meta mining its stuff and, god forbid, finding deals. Will Muse even be able to access price information when the robots.txt of every merchant has a line explicitly telling it to buzz off? body_text: Join us this morning in raising a cup of ambition to celebrate the inaugural “Dolly Parton Day.” The 25th of September (9/25) ((nine-two-five, for those already mentally checked out for the weekend)) has been officially recognized to commemorate the star by the state of California, cities from Nashville to Manhattan, and various counties across the US. Naturally, participants are encouraged to honor Dolly by spreading kindness, wearing pink, and listening to “9 to 5” at 5 p.m. local time, wherever they are celebrating. It’s difficult to imagine anyone on earth more dedicated to Olive Garden than Braden “Breadsticks” Sinclair, a man who has embarked on an “ infinite tour of Italy ” via the Orlando-founded chain, having picked up an exclusive lifetime pasta pass seven years ago. The 33-year-old father of two has set up a website to monitor his mission since then, and has spent the equivalent of $2,100 (and around 170,000 calories) on Olive Garden pasta dishes. The only group who might give Sinclair a run for his money where reliance on the chain famed for its unlimited breadsticks is concerned? Any exec or shareholder with an active investment in Darden Restaurants . For the three-month period through August 30, 2026 (the first quarter of Darden’s fiscal 2027), Olive Garden accounted for around 42% of the restaurant group’s total revenue, even as the chain was forced to abandon a marketing campaign around its soup and salad offerings as cyclospora concerns grew. Meanwhile, LongHorn Steakhouse (again) was growing quicker than any other chain for Darden, with there being 29 more company-owned LongHorns in the world during the Darden’s fiscal first quarter compared to last year and same-store sales rising 6.2%. Olive Garden might still be the biggest brand in its parent company’s portfolio as it enters a new fiscal year, but Darden might not be able to keep relying on the Italian chain to keep investors happy. Indeed, although the OG saw same-store sales show some growth – up 1.1% – in Q1 2027, it wasn’t as much as shareholders had expected, and shares slumped on the results. However, thanks to some smoothing over on Darden’s earnings call later — the company’s CEO partly blamed the World Cup (??) for suppressed sales in the first quarter — the stock recovered some of its initial losses. Lian Yunzhi, a six-year-old speedcuber from China, recently broke the women’s world record for solving a 3x3x3 cube, clocking an average time of just 4.52 seconds across five separate solves. Within three days, Yunzhi had done it again, posting an average solve time of 4.27 seconds at a separate event certified by the World Cube Association, the official governing body of the twisty puzzle scene. While times like that might make a mere mortal of the cubing world’s mind Boggle (different grid-based activity, sorry), there are, it seems, levels to this game. Yunzhi’s parents told China Central Television that she practices two to three hours each day and has mastered over 1,300 solves or “algorithms.” It brings me no pleasure to reveal to our older readers — anyone over the age of around 10, in this specific case — that speedcubing seems to be a young person’s game in 2026, with the overall record for a single solve (2.76 seconds) set by a nine-year-old in February this year .
